Efficient Test-Time Finetuning of LLMs via Convex Reconstruction and Gradient Caching

Alaa Khamis Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: University of Haifa    Alaa Maalouf Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: University of Haifa
Abstract

Test-time finetuning (TTFT) is a rapidly evolving paradigm that adapts a language model to each prompt by retrieving related sequences, updating the model on them, and then evaluating the prompt. However, TTFT is only practical if it is fast: selection and finetuning both happen per query, making each a direct bottleneck. Existing methods trade speed for quality: fast retrieval is often redundant, while stronger diversity-aware selection adds prohibitive per-query cost. We introduce HullFT11 1 Code available at https://github.com/alaa-khamis/HullFT., a geometric approach to TTFT that addresses both bottlenecks. Given a query, HullFT first represents the query embedding as a sparse convex combination of few training sequences, using efficient projection-free Frank–Wolfe optimization. This yields a support set that is inherently relevant and diverse. We then convert the fractional convex weights into an exact integer multiset for finetuning through a geometric integerization procedure. The resulting multiplicities naturally create repeated examples, which we exploit with Gradient Reuse to amortize forward–backward computation across repeated finetuning steps. Our experiments show that HullFT improves the quality–efficiency tradeoff over current state-of-the-art TTFT methods, achieving lower bits-per-byte at substantially lower total runtime.

1 Introduction

Large language models are trained on web-scale corpora and optimized for broad, general-purpose performance across a vast distribution of text [1, 2]. As a result, their weights represent a global optimum that is unlikely to be locally optimal for any specific input. Test-time training (TTT) [3, 4, 5, 6, 7], also referred to as test-time finetuning (TTFT) in recent influential work [8], addresses this directly: at inference time, given a prompt qq, we retrieve the NN most relevant sequences from a large corpus, take one gradient step per retrieved sequence, and evaluate the finetuned model on qq. Retrieving as few as 20 neighbors is enough to substantially close the gap between models differing by more than an order of magnitude in parameter count [5].

Data selection for TTFT runs per prompt at inference time, making it a direct contributor to user-facing latency. Current methods sit at opposite ends of a quality–efficiency tradeoff. Pure nearest-neighbor retrieval [5] returns the top-NN candidates (nearest neighbors in some embedding space) via a FAISS index [9]: fast, but blind to redundancy. On large corpora, duplicate content is common [10, 11]; without accounting for redundancy, the top-NN neighbors can collapse to near-identical sequences, causing every subsequent gradient step to repeat the same signal. Diversity-aware selection methods address this by explicitly penalizing redundancy when choosing examples [8], producing more informative batches. The improvement in bits-per-byte (bpb) [12] over pure retrieval is significant, though such greedy selection introduces overhead, especially at lower NN values.

Novelty. In this work, we take a different route, drawing on provable sparse convex approximation. The key idea is that directions in the embedding space carry meaning: sequences spanning different directions cover a broader range of semantic features, while sequences pointing in nearly the same direction are largely redundant [13, 14]. Thus, framing data selection as a convex approximation of the prompt qq means diversity is inherently derived from the geometry, without explicit penalty terms, greedy heuristics, or expensive search and heavy gradient descent based optimization methods. Once a candidate is selected to help reconstruct qq, near-duplicates pointing in the same direction are naturally down-weighted, as they offer little additional value. The optimization naturally (inherently from the convex approximation definition) turns to unexplored directions instead, covering the prompt’s context (in the embedding space) more broadly [15, 16].

Approximating qq as a convex combination of candidates is precisely the approximate Carathéodory problem [17, 18, 19]: find a small support set with positive weights summing to 11 whose weighted centroid is close to qq. The approximate Carathéodory theorem guarantees that an ε\varepsilon-accurate solution (in squared ℓ2\ell_{2} error) using O⁡(1/ε)O(1/\varepsilon) points always exists, regardless of ambient dimension [17]. This gives us a principled way to obtain a sparse, relevance-aware, and diversity-aware representation of the query from a kNN candidate pool. Notably, convex reconstruction alone does not yet specify a TTFT update sequence. It returns fractional weights over selected examples, while TTFT requires an explicit set of NN samples. We therefore convert the weighted solution into integer multiplicities that preserve the geometric approximation as closely as possible, see more details in Sec. C.1.

Crucially, this discrete reconstruction does more than make the method executable. Once the fractional weights are converted into integers, some selected examples appear multiple times in the final multiset. These repetitions create an opportunity for efficient finetuning: rather than recomputing a fresh forward–backward pass for every repeated occurrence, we can reuse cached gradients across short runs of identical examples. Thus, integerization not only bridges geometry and TTFT, but also induces the structure that enables Gradient Reuse. Figure 1 summarizes the HullFT pipeline.

Our contributions. We introduce HullFT, an efficient test-time finetuning method that improves the quality–efficiency tradeoff of TTFT through three coupled ideas.

  1. 1.

    We formulate query/prompts-specific data selection as a sparse convex approximation problem over a kNN-retrieved candidate pool, yielding a support set that is both relevant and diverse. We suggest solving it using the Frank–Wolfe algorithm. This efficient projection-free convex approximation procedure selects a small, diverse, and relevant support set from the candidate pool (Alg. 3 in the appendix).

  2. 2.

    We introduce a geometric integerization procedure (Alg. 1) that turns fractional convex weights into an exact NN-example training multiset while preserving approximation quality.

  3. 3.

    We show that the resulting multiset (from 2) enables Gradient Reuse, which amortizes gradient computation across repeated training examples and reduces finetuning cost (Alg. 4).

Across 12 subsets of The Pile [12], HullFT strictly outperforms our competing methods (kNN [5] and SIFT [8]) on quality–efficiency tradeoffs, with the largest gains in the latency-critical regime.

2 Related work

Test-time training and finetuning. Instance-specific adaptation traces back to transductive learning [20] and has recently re-emerged as test-time training (TTT), where deep networks adapt at inference time using self-supervised objectives [3, 4, 6, 7]. For language models, nearest-neighbor TTT finetunes on retrieved examples [5], while SIFT adds an information-theoretic selection criterion that accounts for redundancy [8]. Alternatively, retrieval-augmented models place retrieved text in context [21, 22], but self-attention cost limits context size and full benefits often require retrieval-aware training [5]. Related selection methods balance relevance and diversity via maximal marginal relevance or determinantal point processes [13, 14]. Influence-based methods estimate example utility [23, 24], including through gradient similarity for LLM finetuning [25, 26, 27], but typically score points independently and thus miss redundancy [8]. Active learning selects diverse subsets to cover the data manifold [15, 16], but is not query-conditioned.

Data selection. Early transfer-learning work showed that an additional finetuning stage on in-domain text produces large gains across tasks [28, 29]. The approach has since been validated in biomedicine [30, 31, 32], scientific text [33], legal language [34], and clinical question answering [35], establishing domain-specific adaptation as a default recipe. Beyond the choice of domain, the composition of the training subset itself can be decisive: a handful of curated examples sometimes matches full-corpus finetuning [36], parameter-efficient methods make per-task adaptation practical even for very large models [37], and recent work explicitly optimizes which data to include for specialization [38, 39]. Adaptation benefits extend beyond language; for instance, they have been shown to govern out-of-distribution robustness in vision-based driving [40, 41]. At the pre-training scale, a parallel effort in data curation tackles redundancy through deduplication, quality filtering, and domain reweighting [10, 11, 42, 43, 1, 2]. Our approach pushes this logic to its extreme: rather than curating a training set once, we curate query-specific subsets at inference time, using convex geometry to jointly enforce relevance and diversity within a single optimization.

Convex approximation, Frank–Wolfe, and coresets. Carathéodory’s theorem [18] guarantees that any point in the convex hull of a set in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} can be written as a convex combination of at most d+1d{+}1 points, requiring O⁡(n2​d)O(n^{2}d) time for constructing such a set. Lately,  [44] proposed a fast construction running in O⁡(n​d+d4​log⁡n)O(nd+d^{4}\log n) time. The approximate variant relaxes this to O⁡(1/ε2)O(1/\varepsilon^{2}) points independent of dimension [45, 17, 46]. The Frank–Wolfe (conditional gradient) algorithm [47, 48] provides a constructive proof of this result, with each iteration being a sparse convex combination that grows by at most one point [19]. Other variants achieve faster convergence under favorable geometry [49, 50]. The connection between Frank–Wolfe and coresets (small weighted subsets that provably approximate a cost function over the full data) was established by Clarkson [51] and developed in a rich body of work on geometric data summarization [52, 53, 54]. In machine learning, coreset methods have been applied to regression [44, 55], data-efficient model training and subset selection for deep learning [16, 15, 56, 57, 58, 59], model compression and network pruning [60, 61, 62, 63], and general-purpose loss approximation under unified coreset frameworks [64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 69]. Our selection stage instantiates Frank–Wolfe on the ℓ2\ell_{2}-squared objective over the probability simplex, yielding a coreset of the candidate pool. Integerization then converts into a multiset for finetuning.

3 Method

Notation. Let ⟨u,v⟩=u⊤​v\langle u,v\rangle=u^{\top}v be the dot product on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, 𝟏​[⋅]\mathbf{1}[\cdot] the indicator function (𝟏​[A]=1\mathbf{1}[A]=1 if predicate AA is true, 00 otherwise), ΔK\Delta^{K} the probability simplex in ℝK\mathbb{R}^{K}, and ei∈ℝKe_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} the ii-th standard basis vector. We use q∈ℝdq\in\mathbb{R}^{d} to denote a query, {p1,…,pK}⊂ℝd\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{K}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} to denote a candidate training pool, and P∈ℝd×KP\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times K} to denote the matrix whose ii-th column is pip_{i}, so P​w=∑iwi​piPw=\sum_{i}w_{i}\,p_{i} for any w∈ℝKw\in\mathbb{R}^{K} (all in the embedding space). The final selected support set is S={s1,…,s|S|}⊆{p1,…,pK}S=\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{|S|}\}\subseteq\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{K}\}, with associated integer counts c∈ℤ≥0|S|c\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{|S|}, where cjc_{j} is the count of sjs_{j}. 3.1 Data selection via convex approximation

Frank–Wolfe support set. From the preselected pool of KK candidates, we solve the approximate Carathéodory problem by running the Frank–Wolfe (conditional gradient) algorithm [47, 48] on the ℓ2\ell_{2}-squared objective over the probability simplex (Alg. 3). Selection reduces to finding a sparse w∈ΔKw\in\Delta^{K} whose convex combination P​wPw approximates qq:

minw∈ΔK⁡‖q−P​w‖22.\min_{w\in\Delta^{K}}\;\|q-Pw\|_{2}^{2}. (1)

The support of ww is the selected subset: pip_{i} is picked iff wi>0w_{i}>0. The method is projection-free, requires only inner-product evaluations, and its iterates are sparse convex combinations by design [51].

Starting from the single vertex w=ev⋆w=e_{v^{\star}}, where v⋆=arg⁡maxi∈[K]​⟨q,pi⟩v^{\star}=\arg\max_{i\in[K]}\langle q,p_{i}\rangle, each iteration forms the residual r=q−P​wr=q-Pw, picks the vertex index v=arg⁡maxi∈[K]​⟨r,pi⟩v=\arg\max_{i\in[K]}\langle r,p_{i}\rangle, and takes an exact line search along the edge from ww to eve_{v}. A step adds at most one new nonzero to ww, so iterates stay sparse throughout, and near-duplicates barely move the residual and are naturally skipped. We stop as soon as ‖q−P​w‖22≤ε\|q-Pw\|_{2}^{2}\leq\varepsilon or |{i:wi>0}|=m|\{i:w_{i}>0\}|=m, whichever comes first. The cap mm is the binding constraint in practice: left alone, FW keeps adding vertices and ww eventually fills in over most of the pool. The algorithm is defined in the appendix, Sec. B.1 as Alg. 3; we spell out Frank–Wolfe for completeness.

Geometric integerization. Frank–Wolfe (Alg. 3) returns fractional weights, which cannot be used directly for finetuning. Training on a uniformly weighted subset can outperform loss reweighting, which is prone to variance amplification and overfitting to noisy samples [70]. We therefore convert the fractional weights into integer counts that define an equally weighted multiset, preserving the geometric approximation quality (Alg. 1).

Write the indices of the nonzero entries of ww as {i1,…,i|S|}:={j∣wj>0}\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{|S|}\}:=\{j\mid w_{j}>0\}, let S:={s1,…,s|S|}={pj∣wj>0}S:=\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{|S|}\}=\{p_{j}\mid w_{j}>0\} be the corresponding chosen points from Alg. 3, and for every j∈{1,…,|S|}j\in\{1,\ldots,|S|\}, let w~j:=wij\tilde{w}_{j}:=w_{i_{j}}. We look for integer counts c∈ℤ≥0|S|c\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{|S|} with ∑jcj=N\sum_{j}c_{j}=N minimizing the reconstruction error

‖q−∑j=1|S|cjN​sj‖22,\Bigl\|q-\sum_{j=1}^{|S|}\tfrac{c_{j}}{N}\,s_{j}\Bigr\|_{2}^{2}, (2)

i.e. the NN-point multiset over SS whose uniform mean is closest to qq. Turning the continuous weights into discrete counts is tricky because the rounded multiset must satisfy two constraints at once: it must contain exactly NN examples, and its empirical mean should remain close to the Frank–Wolfe convex combination. We therefore view integerization as a small discrete reconstruction problem around the continuous solution. The three steps below progressively restore feasibility and reduce the same geometric objective in Eq. 2:

  1. 1.

    Floor allocation: We start by setting cj=⌊N​w~j⌋c_{j}=\lfloor N\tilde{w}_{j}\rfloor. This gives each point the number of copies suggested by its Frank–Wolfe weight, while making sure we do not exceed the budget. Very small-weight points naturally get zero copies at this stage.

  2. 2.

    Greedy fill: Rounding down leaves a few unallocated copies. We add them one at a time to the point that most reduces the reconstruction error in Eq. 2, so the leftover budget is used to repair the geometric shift introduced by flooring.

  3. 3.

    Local-swap refinement: Finally, we check whether moving one copy from one support point to another improves the reconstruction. This keeps the budget fixed, but corrects small rounding mistakes left by the greedy fill. We run this pairwise check for two passes.

After this, each support point sjs_{j} is included cjc_{j} times to form the final multiset of exactly NN sequences.

Full selection algorithm. Combining both steps, the selection pipeline (Alg. 2) takes the candidate pool and budget and returns the final training multiset.

3.2 Efficient finetuning via gradient reuse

The integerized multiset contains repeated sequences: a support point sjs_{j} with count cjc_{j} appears cjc_{j} times in the finetuning batch. A naïve implementation treats these copies as independent samples and performs a separate forward-backward pass for each one, causing the computational cost to scale linearly with NN regardless of duplication. We exploit the integer multiplicities produced by geometric integerization to amortize gradient computation across repeated optimizer steps (Alg. 4). Rather than recomputing the gradient at every repeated step on sjs_{j}, we cache and reuse gradients: we refresh g~\tilde{g} once every rr steps and apply the cached value for the intermediate r−1r{-}1 updates. Let t=0,1,…,cj−1t=0,1,\ldots,c_{j}-1 index the repeated steps on sjs_{j}:

g~t={∇θℒ​(θt,sj)if ​tmodr=0,g~t−1otherwise,θt+1=AdamStep​(θt,g~t,η).\tilde{g}_{t}=\begin{cases}\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta_{t};\,s_{j})&\text{if }t\bmod r=0,\\ \tilde{g}_{t-1}&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}\qquad\theta_{t+1}=\textsc{AdamStep}(\theta_{t},\,\tilde{g}_{t},\,\eta). (3)

This reduces forward-backward passes from NN to ⌈N/r⌉\lceil N/r\rceil. For small refresh intervals rr, the parameter drift between consecutive steps on identical input is mild enough that reusing a cached gradient preserves convergence quality (see Sec. 4). The full gradient-reuse procedure is defined in Sec. B.1 as Alg. 4. For gradient reuse to work, all copies of a given sequence must appear consecutively in the training order. Integerization gives this property by construction: multiplicities are fixed upfront, so each unique text is trained for all its cjc_{j} steps in a single consecutive block. We test whether this structure can be imposed on SIFT in Sec. 4.

4 Experimental results

The setup. We evaluate on 12 subsets of The Pile [12] using GPT-2 [71]. For each subset, we average the results over 150 test queries. All methods share a K=200K{=}200 nearest-neighbor candidate pool retrieved via a precomputed FAISS index. Following [8], we use the normalized RoBERTa encoder for embeddings and finetune with Adam (l​r=5×10−5lr{=}5{\times}10^{-5}). Experiments run on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, except for the CPU evaluation in Sec. 4. Our metric is Bits-Per-Byte (BPB%) relative to a non-finetuned baseline. Since TTFT happens at inference time, we report the BPB% achievable within a given total-runtime budget TT (selection + finetuning), sweeping N∈[1,50]N\in[1,50]. For more details, see Appendix A and Appendix C for extended experiments and ablations, which cover FW and Carathéodory selection variants, kNN candidate pool sizing, and qualitative selection comparisons.

Quality–runtime tradeoff. We compare HullFT against SIFT[8], which selects examples to reduce response uncertainty by optimizing information gain while accounting for information duplication, and kNN[5], which finetunes on top-NN nearest neighbors, across a range of total-runtime budgets TT. Figure 2 reports the average BPB% across all datasets as a function of total runtime, together with the BPB% gap between HullFT and the best baseline available at each budget. Table 1 reports the corresponding per-subset BPB% values at the two representative budgets T=1.75​sT{=}1.75s and T=2.0​sT{=}2.0s. Across every total-runtime budget T≤4​sT\!\leq\!4s , our method achieves a strictly lower BPB% than both SIFT and kNN. The gap over the best baseline is largest at tight budgets: 6.4%\mathbf{6.4\%} lower at T=0.75​sT{=}0.75s, 3.8%\mathbf{3.8\%} lower at T=1.75​sT{=}1.75s, 3.4%\mathbf{3.4\%} lower at T=2.0​sT{=}2.0s, and closes only once our method saturates its NN budget near 3.8​s3.8s. In the latency-critical TTFT regime, where every additional second of total runtime is visible in user-facing latency, our method is Pareto-dominant. Figure 2 (right) plots this best-baseline gap continuously as a function of TT: our method dominates the strongest competing baseline for every T≲4.5​sT\!\lesssim\!4.5s and the margin grows as the budget tightens, exactly the regime a latency-sensitive deployment cares about.

Per-subset breakdown. We test whether the aggregate runtime advantage is driven by a few favorable subsets or appears broadly across The Pile. Figure 3 shows the full per-subset quality–runtime curves and best-baseline gaps. Table 1 shows per-subset BPB% for kNN, SIFT, and HullFT at T=1.75​sT{=}1.75s (kNN N⋆=15N^{\star}{=}15, SIFT N⋆=11N^{\star}{=}11, HullFT N⋆=19N^{\star}{=}19) and at T=2.0​sT{=}2.0s (kNN N⋆=17N^{\star}{=}17, SIFT N⋆=13N^{\star}{=}13, HullFT N⋆=22N^{\star}{=}22), using the N⋆N^{\star} each method attains in our sweep for that time budget. At T=1.75​sT{=}1.75s, our method improves over the best performing baseline on 11 of 12 subsets, with an average margin of 3.83%3.83\%; at T=2.0​sT{=}2.0s the same holds, with an average margin of 3.44%3.44\% (as in Fig. 2). The quality gap is largest on subsets where finetuning signal continues to improve with larger multisets (Enron, GitHub, USPTO, NIH), which is exactly where our method’s ability to reach a higher N⋆N^{\star} within the same time budget matters most. The mechanism is a two-stage speedup: our selection stage is 8.8×\mathbf{8.8\times} faster than SIFT at N=50N{=}50 (0.059​s0.059s vs 0.524​s0.524s, the saturation point our method reaches near T≈3.8​sT{\approx}3.8s) and over 𝟏𝟐×\mathbf{12\times} faster averaged across N∈[1,50]N\!\in\![1,50], and Gradient Reuse further cuts finetuning by 1.48×\mathbf{1.48\times} (Tab. 2). These speedups compound so that, inside a given time budget, our method can afford a substantially larger N⋆N^{\star}, and the extra multiset mass more than offsets matched-NN quality differences relative to the baselines. Against kNN at matched NN (Fig. 8), our BPB% is lower at every N≥10N\!\geq\!10: pure nearest-neighbour retrieval saturates because its top-kk is redundant under the query embedding, whereas the convex-hull support set keeps adding signal.

Gradient reuse ablation. Table 2 isolates the effect of Gradient Reuse on our method at N=50N{=}50. Averaged over 12 subsets, GR yields a 1.48×\mathbf{1.48\times} finetuning speedup at a cost of only 0.64%0.64\% of average BPB%. On subsets where integerization produces few repeats (GitHub, Enron) GR is effectively a no-op both in runtime and quality, while on subsets with many repeats the speedup is substantially larger. This is what enables the compounded savings that Fig. 2 and Tab. 1 rely on. Appendix Appendix C shows the BPB-versus-NN comparison across all three methods for N∈{1,…,50}N\in\{1,\dots,50\}. Figure 4 ablates the gradient refresh interval rr, where r=1r{=}1 is the standard finetuning without GR; r=2r{=}2 already delivers a substantial runtime reduction at a very low BPB% cost, while r=3r{=}3 saves further wall time at a more noticeable quality cost. We adopt r=2r{=}2 as our default for the best speedup–accuracy tradeoff.

SIFT gradient reuse experiment. We investigate whether Gradient Reuse can be applied to other selection methods to improve their efficiency. While kNN retrieval [5] returns NN distinct sequences without repetitions, SIFT [8] can revisit the same sequence at non-consecutive steps. To enable Gradient Reuse for SIFT, we evaluate two modified schedules: global deduplication, which collapses all occurrences of each unique text into a single block with aggregated counts, and consecutive grouping, which merges only adjacent duplicates. Figure 5 reports the BPB%–runtime behavior of these SIFT reuse variants across selection budgets, with HullFT included for reference. Table 3 reports the same comparison at N=50N{=}50, averaged over the 12 Pile subsets.

The results show that Gradient Reuse accelerates SIFT, presenting a clear quality–efficiency tradeoff. Global deduplication provides a substantial speedup but alters the original training order, increasing the BPB%. Consecutive grouping preserves the schedule better, yielding a smaller runtime gain with minimal quality degradation. Unlike SIFT, HullFT inherently produces repeated contiguous blocks during integerization, allowing it to fully exploit Gradient Reuse without post-hoc reordering.

CPU-only evaluation. We repeat the N=20N{=}20 comparison on CPU only over 6 Pile subsets (ArXiv, DM Mathematics, Enron, FreeLaw, GitHub, HackerNews). Figure 6 reports mean CPU selection time, finetuning time, total runtime, and BPB% for kNN, SIFT, and HullFT. HullFT’s FW selector is 25.8×\mathbf{25.8\times} faster than SIFT’s on CPU (0.036​s0.036s vs. 0.934​s0.934s). Because Gradient Reuse reduces the number of forward-backward passes, finetuning is also faster: 228.4​s228.4s vs. 317.4​s317.4s for kNN and 318.4​s318.4s for SIFT, saving roughly 𝟖𝟗​𝐬\mathbf{89s} end-to-end. On BPB%, HullFT (72.05%72.05\%) is close to kNN (72.78%72.78\%) and within 2.3%2.3\% of SIFT (69.78%69.78\%), while being substantially faster end-to-end (Fig. 6).

Selection diversity. Figure 7 visualizes, for a representative ArXiv query at N=20N{=}20, the support sets chosen by kNN, SIFT, and HullFT in a 3D t-SNE projection of the candidate pool. kNN concentrates its budget in a tight neighborhood of the query, while SIFT places its points more broadly around the query to reduce redundancy. HullFT yields a comparably diverse support, obtained directly from the geometry of the convex approximation in Sec. 3 rather than from any explicit diversity term. This diversity is achieved at a fraction of SIFT’s per-query selection cost (Sec. 4), consistent with our central thesis that geometric reconstruction recovers a comparably diverse selection at substantially lower latency.

More results. The appendix provides extended experiments and results. Specifically, Appendix C includes a comprehensive sweep of the budget NN, integerization ablations, Carathéodory variants comparisons, and sensitivity analyses for ε\varepsilon, rr, and kk. We also provide per-subset breakdowns (Sec. C.6), qualitative results, and text examples (Sec. C.9).

5 Conclusion and Limitations

We introduced HullFT, a test-time finetuning pipeline that frames data selection as sparse convex approximation of the query embedding over a candidate pool. Frank–Wolfe yields a diverse, relevance-aware support set without explicit redundancy penalties, geometric integerization converts the resulting fractional weights into an exact NN-point training multiset, and Gradient Reuse amortizes the repeated optimizer steps this multiset produces. Across 12 subsets of The Pile, HullFT attains a strictly lower BPB% than both kNN retrieval and SIFT at every total-runtime budget T≤4​sT\!\leq\!4s , with the margin widening as the budget tightens. The gains come from a compounded two-stage speedup (selection is 12×12\times faster than SIFT on average and Gradient Reuse cuts finetuning by 1.48×1.48\times), which lets HullFT reach a substantially larger effective NN inside a fixed latency budget. These results suggest that convex geometry is a natural vehicle for latency-constrained test-time adaptation, and that the integer structure it induces opens further room for optimizer-level amortization.

Limitations. Similarly to SIFT [8], HullFT operates over a kNN-preselected candidate pool rather than the full corpus: the convex approximation is only as expressive as the directions present in this pool, so the quality of the support set ultimately inherits the recall ceiling of the upstream retriever and embedding model. Second, selection runs in a fixed embedding space decoupled from the base LLM: this keeps the method general and model-agnostic, but the geometry is not tailored to the loss landscape of the model being adapted, leaving potential per-model gains on the table.

Appendix A Experimental protocol details

The main experiments use 12 Pile subsets and 150 test queries per subset. This protocol is a compute-conscious version of the evaluation style used by TTT-NN [5] and SIFT [8], which evaluate approximately 1%1\% of the full Pile test set (18121812 points) and report only on subsets with more than 10 test examples. We use the larger fixed per-subset sample because our goal is not only to report a single aggregate number, but also to understand whether HullFT’s runtime–quality behavior is stable across domains with different redundancy patterns. A balanced 150-query sample gives each subset enough weight for per-domain comparisons while keeping the full sweep over methods, budgets, and ablations feasible on our available A100 compute.

We build and use precomputed per-subset retrieval pools rather than a single live global index. This keeps the comparison focused on the TTFT components studied in the paper: query-conditioned selection from a shared candidate pool and the subsequent finetuning schedule. All methods receive the same KK precomputed nearest neighbors for each query, so retrieval differences cannot explain the reported gaps. We also exclude pool retrieval time from the main runtime measurements because it is identical across methods once the candidate pool is fixed; selection and finetuning are the parts changed by HullFT. For context, Hardt and Sun [5] report mean distributed Pile retrieval time of 1.35​s1.35s (std. 0.12​s0.12s).

Unless otherwise stated, all main experiments use normalized RoBERTa embeddings from socialfoundations/roberta-large-pile-lr2e-5-bs16-8gpu-1700000, GPT-2 as the adapted model, Adam with learning rate 5×10−55{\times}10^{-5}, K=200K{=}200 preselected candidates, and selection budgets N∈{1,…,50}N\in\{1,\ldots,50\}.

Appendix B Algorithmic details

This section provides pseudocode for the core procedures, algorithmic variants, and baselines referenced in Sec. 3. The variants modify individual stages of the HullFT pipeline.

B.1 Core HullFT procedures

Algorithm 3 and Alg. 4 give the procedures referenced in Sec. 3. Frank–Wolfe is a classical conditional-gradient method [47, 48]; we include its specialization to our objective for completeness, not as a new algorithmic contribution.

B.2 Exact Carathéodory reduction

The exact Carathéodory theorem guarantees that any point in the convex hull of a set in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} can be expressed as a convex combination of at most d+1d+1 points. Algorithm 5 implements the standard constructive procedure: it iteratively finds an affine dependency among the current support points and eliminates the one that drives a weight to zero, repeating until the size bound d+1d+1 is met.

Figure 10 (see Sec. C.2) compares exact Carathéodory selection against HullFT with different integerization strategies. The key finding is that geometric integerization is essential: padding Carathéodory weights directly is unstable as NN grows, while FW with geometric integerization (HullFT) matches or beats the best Carathéodory variant at lower selection cost.

B.3 PCA-reduced convex approximation

When the embedding dimension dd is large, inner-product evaluations inside Frank–Wolfe dominate selection cost. Algorithm 6 mitigates this by projecting the query and candidate pool into a lower-dimensional subspace via PCA before running the geometric selection, then mapping the chosen support back to the original space for integerization.

B.4 Weight-proportional padding

As a simpler baseline to the full geometric integerization (Alg. 1), Alg. 7 allocates the discrete budget NN proportionally to the fractional weights via largest-remainder rounding, without the subsequent local-swap refinement step.

Figure 9 (see Sec. C.1) compares this simpler baseline against the full geometric integerization used by HullFT.

Appendix C Ablations

This section isolates the effect of individual design choices. Each ablation sweeps one axis while holding the rest of the pipeline fixed to the configuration used in Sec. 4.

For completeness, Fig. 8 reports BPB% as a function of the selection budget NN across the three main methods.

C.1 Integerization: pad-by-weights vs. geometric (FW family)

We compare the fractional FW solution (no integerization), FW followed by padding by weights (Alg. 7), and FW followed by the geometric integerization used by HullFT (Alg. 1). Figure 9 reports BPB% for these three FW-based variants both as a function of selection budget NN and as a function of total runtime. The right panel shows the same comparison on a total-runtime x-axis: since all three variants share the same FW selection stage, the runtime difference is negligible and quality vs time differences are the dominant effect.

C.2 Carathéodory selection and its integerizations

Replacing FW with exact Carathéodory (Alg. 5) yields a fractional solution with at most d+1d{+}1 points; we compare its pad-by-weights and geometric integerizations against HullFT. Figure 10 reports BPB% for these Carathéodory-based variants and HullFT, plotted against both selection budget and total runtime. Geometric integerization is essential: padding Carathéodory weights directly is unstable as NN grows. The right panel makes the runtime cost of exact Carathéodory visible: its selection time is roughly 14×14\times higher than FW, so even when its BPB% at matched NN is competitive, HullFT dominates on the total-runtime axis.

C.3 Frank–Wolfe tolerance ε\varepsilon

We sweep the FW stopping tolerance ε∈{0,10−8,10−5,10−2,10−1}\varepsilon\in\{0,10^{-8},10^{-5},10^{-2},10^{-1}\} for HullFT and for the Carathéodory-integerized variant. Figure 11 reports BPB% under this tolerance sweep at N=20N{=}20 and N=50N{=}50. The x-axis is inverted: the left end is the loosest tolerance (ε=10−1\varepsilon{=}10^{-1}) and the right end is the exact solution (ε=0\varepsilon{=}0), so moving right means strictly tighter convergence. HullFT’s BPB% is flat across the entire range up through ε=10−2\varepsilon{=}10^{-2}, indicating that the support cap mm, not the tolerance, is the binding constraint in practice. Meanwhile, the Carathéodory variant degrades noticeably once ε>10−5\varepsilon{>}10^{-5}, justifying the moderate tolerance used in the main experiments.

C.4 FW variant: forced-unique selection without ε\varepsilon early-stop

We ask whether the ε\varepsilon early-stop and the allowance for point revisits in standard HullFT are important. The fw_no_epsilon variant disables the ε\varepsilon early-stop and forces each FW iteration to select a previously unchosen point. When FW keeps adding distinct points, the weights assigned to them become spread thinly, so many of the selected points carry negligible weight and contribute little information. Geometric integerization handles this gracefully: by selecting only the most important points from the support, it recovers performance on par with standard HullFT. Variants that use the full point set without this selection step do not benefit from the additional points and perform noticeably worse. Table 4 reports total runtime and BPB% relative to the non-finetuned baseline at N∈{20,25,30,35}N\in\{20,25,30,35\}; all four variants are within 0.15​s0.15s of each other.

C.5 kNN pre-selection pool size kk

We vary the pre-selection pool kk fed to the three selectors at two representative budgets N∈{20,50}N\in\{20,50\}. Figure 12 reports BPB% as the pre-selection pool size varies at each of these budgets. All methods improve slightly with larger kk, with returns saturating by k=500k{=}500; HullFT stays strictly between kNN and SIFT at matched NN and remains Pareto-dominant on total runtime at every kk.

C.6 Per-subset breakdown against each baseline individually

Figure 3 in the main text reports the per-subset gap against the best of kNN and SIFT at each budget. For completeness, Figs. 13 and 14 show the same breakdown against each baseline in isolation, so the reader can see where HullFT’s advantage comes from kNN vs. SIFT separately. At each anchor TT, N⋆N^{\star} is taken from the global aggregate (matching Tab. 1) and per-subset BPB% is read at those fixed N⋆N^{\star} values.

C.7 Fidelity of geometric integerization to Frank–Wolfe weights

Frank–Wolfe produces fractional weights on a sparse support; geometric integerization converts these into an exact NN-tuple of pool indices with multiplicities cic_{i}, so the induced empirical weights are w^i=ci/N\hat{w}_{i}=c_{i}/N on that same support. We quantify how much the discrete allocation departs from the pre-integerization FW vector by the per-query distance ‖𝐰−𝐰^‖2\|\mathbf{w}-\hat{\mathbf{w}}\|_{2}, averaged over all test queries in each subset. Fig. 15 reports the mean of these averages across the twelve Pile subsets for which we precomputed embeddings (shaded band: ±\pm one standard deviation across subsets). The distance stays in a moderate range for every N≤50N\leq 50, which supports the view that integerization preserves the FW weight profile rather than inducing an unrelated discrete selection.

C.8 Selection geometry: t-SNE visualizations

We extend the qualitative analysis of the main text to two additional subsets, GitHub and FreeLaw, which exhibit different candidate-pool structure. Figure 16 shows a 3D t-SNE projection of the query, candidate pool, and the N=20N{=}20 points returned by kNN, SIFT, and HullFT on a representative query from each subset. The pattern observed for ArXiv recurs: kNN clusters tightly around the query, SIFT places its points more broadly around the query to reduce redundancy, and HullFT produces a comparably diverse support obtained directly from the convex approximation in Sec. 3. Because the same behavior appears across pools with markedly different topology, the diversity is most plausibly attributable to the geometric mechanism itself rather than to properties specific to a single domain. This diversity is achieved at a fraction of SIFT’s per-query selection cost (Sec. 4), reinforcing the headline efficiency–quality tradeoff reported in the main text.

C.9 Qualitative examples of selected contexts

For two representative test queries in each of ArXiv, GitHub, and PubMed Central, we show the test query alongside the two candidates with the largest weight in the HullFT support at N=20N{=}20. All text below is verbatim from the Pile candidate pool; we truncate each excerpt to roughly 400 characters for readability.

ArXiv.

prompt The operational meaning of quantum conditional information. Information might be regarded as an answer to a question. To know if it is raining, one need only look outside. However, a person living in a desert would expect a different answer than one living in a climate where on average, it rains every other day. After looking outside, who gains “more” information? The answer to this question has nothing to do with weather …\dots
Example 1 Every forecasting system is noncalibrated for uncountably many data sequences that it might see. This result is strengthened here: from a topological point of view, failure of calibration is typical and calibration rare. Meanwhile, Bayesian forecasters are certain that they are calibrated—this invites worries about the connection between Bayesianism and rationality. …\dots
Example 2 Landauer’s erasure principle exposes an intrinsic relation between thermodynamics and information theory: the erasure of information stored in a system, SS, requires an amount of work proportional to the entropy of that system. This entropy, H⁡(S|O)H(S|O), depends on the information that a given observer, OO, has about SS …\dots
